18            Plaintiff Miriam Rodriguez, individually, and on behalf of all others
19    similarly situated, brings this Class Action Complaint (“Complaint”) against
20    Defendant Credit Sesame, Inc. (“Credit Sesame” or “Defendant”), to obtain
21    damages, restitution, and injunctive relief for the Class, as defined below, from
22    Defendant. Plaintiff makes the following allegations on information and belief,
23    except as to her own actions, which are made on personal knowledge, the
24    investigation of counsel, and the facts that are a matter of public record.
25                                     INTRODUCTION
26            1.   This class action arises out of the recent targeted ransomware attack
27    and data breach (“Data Breach”) on Defendant’s network that resulted in
28    unauthorized access to the highly sensitive data of Plaintiff and Class members. As

                                    CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
        Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF       Document 1     Filed 04/23/25   Page 2 of 38




1    a result of the Data Breach, Class Members suffered ascertainable losses in the
2    form of the benefit of their bargain, out-of-pocket expenses, and the value of their
3    time reasonably incurred to remedy or mitigate the effects of the attack, emotional
4    distress, and the present risk of imminent harm caused by the compromise of their
5    sensitive personal information.
6             2.   Upon information and belief, the specific information compromised in
7    the Data Breach includes, but is not limited to, personally identifiable information
8    (“PII”).
9             3.   Upon information and belief, up to and through April 2025, Defendant
10   obtained the PII of Plaintiff and Class Members and stored that PII, unencrypted,
11   in an Internet-accessible environment on Defendant’s network, from which
12   unauthorized actors used an extraction tool to retrieve sensitive PII belonging to
13   Plaintiff and Class Members.
14            4.   Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII—which were entrusted to
15   Defendant, their officials, and agents—were compromised and unlawfully accessed
16   due to the Data Breach.
17            5.   Plaintiff brings this class action lawsuit on behalf of those similarly
18   situated to address Defendant’s inadequate safeguarding of Plaintiff’s and Class
19   Members’ PII that Defendant collected and maintained, and for Defendant’s failure
20   to provide timely and adequate notice to Plaintiff and other Class Members that
21   their PII had been subject to the unauthorized access of an unknown, unauthorized
22   party.
23            6.   Defendant maintained the PII in a negligent and/or reckless manner. In
24   particular, the PII was maintained on Defendant’s computer system and network in
25   a condition vulnerable to cyberattacks. Upon information and belief, the
26   mechanism of the cyberattack and potential for improper disclosure of Plaintiff’s
27   and Class Members’ PII was a known risk to Defendant, and thus Defendant was
28                                            2
                                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
        Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF        Document 1     Filed 04/23/25   Page 3 of 38




1    on notice that failing to take steps necessary to secure the PII from those risks left
2    that property in a dangerous condition.
3           7.   In addition, upon information and belief, Defendant and its employees
4    failed to properly monitor the computer network, IT systems, and integrated service
5    that housed Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII.
6           8.   Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ identities are now at risk because of
7    Defendant’s negligent conduct because the PII that Defendant collected and
8    maintained is now in the hands of malicious cybercriminals. The risks to Plaintiff
9    and Class Members will remain for their respective lifetimes.
10          9.   Defendant failed to provide timely, accurate and adequate notice to
11   Plaintiff and Class Members. Plaintiff and Class Members’ knowledge about the
12   PII Defendant lost, as well as precisely what type of information was unencrypted
13   and in the possession of unknown third parties, was unreasonably delayed by
14   Defendant’s failure to warn impacted persons immediately upon learning of the
15   Data Breach.
16          10. Armed with the PII accessed in the Data Breach, data thieves can
17   commit a variety of crimes including opening new financial accounts in Class
18   Members’ names, taking out loans in Class Members’ names, using Class
19   Members’ names to obtain medical services, using Class Members’ information to
20   target other phishing and hacking intrusions using Class Members’ information to
21   obtain government benefits, filing fraudulent tax returns using Class Members’
22   information, obtaining driver’s licenses in Class Members’ names but with another
23   person’s photograph, and giving false information to police during an arrest.
24          11. As a result of the Data Breach, Plaintiff and Class Members have been
25   exposed to a present, heightened and imminent risk of fraud and identity theft.
26   Plaintiff and Class Members must now closely monitor their financial accounts to
27   guard against identity theft for the rest of their lives.
28                                            3
                                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
        Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF      Document 1     Filed 04/23/25   Page 4 of 38




1          12. Plaintiff and Class Members may also incur out of pocket costs for
2    purchasing credit monitoring services, credit freezes, credit reports, or other
3    protective measures to deter and detect identity theft.
4          13. By her Complaint, Plaintiff seeks to remedy these harms on behalf of
5    herself and all similarly situated individuals whose PII was accessed during the
6    Data Breach.
7          14. Accordingly, Plaintiff brings claims on behalf of herself and the Class
8    for: (i) negligence, (ii) breach of implied contract (iii) invasion of privacy (iv)
9    breach of fiduciary duty, and (v) violations of the California Unfair Competition
10   Law. Through these claims, Plaintiff seeks, inter alia, damages and injunctive
11   relief, including improvements to Defendant’s data security systems and integrated
12   services, future annual audits, and adequate credit monitoring services.
13                                        PARTIES
14         15. Plaintiff Miriam Rodriguez is a natural person, resident, and citizen of
15   New Jersey where she intends to remain. She is a Data Breach victim, having been
16   a customer of Defendant.
17         16. Defendant Credit Sesame, Inc., is a stock corporation incorporated
18   under the laws of Delaware and with its principal place of business at 444 Castro
19   Street, Suite 500, Mountain View, CA 94041.
20                            JURISDICTION AND VENUE
21         17. This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action under the
22   Class Action Fairness Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2). The amount in controversy
23   exceeds $5 million, exclusive of interest and costs. Defendant and Plaintiffs are
24   citizens of different states. And there are over 100 putative Class Members.
25         18. This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendant because Credit
26   Sesame has its principal place of business and/or corporate headquarters in
27   California. Furthermore, Defendant regularly conducts business in California and
28                                           4
                                 CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
           Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF           Document 1    Filed 04/23/25   Page 5 of 38




1    have sufficient minimum contacts in California.
2              19. Venue is proper in this Court because Defendant’s principal office is in
3    this District, and because a substantial part of the events, acts, and omissions giving
4    rise to Plaintiffs’ claims occurred in this District.
5                                        BACKGROUND FACTS
6    A.       Defendant’s Businesses
7              20. Defendant is an online financial planning and banking service
8    provider.1
9              21. On information and belief, Defendant maintains the PII of current and
10   former customers, including but not limited to:
11                    a.       name, address, phone number and email address;
12                    b.       date of birth;
13                    c.       Social Security number;
14                    d.       Driver’s license number, passport number, or other state or
15                             government IDs;
16                    e.       Credit or Debit card numbers;
17                    f.       Bankruptcy filings;
18                    g.       Financial statements and financial account numbers;
19                    h.       Credit reports;
20                    i.       Loan applications;
21                    j.       employment information, and;
22                    k.       other information that Defendant may deem necessary to provide
23                             its services.
24             22. Plaintiff and Class Members directly or indirectly entrusted Defendant
25   with sensitive and confidential PII, which includes information that is static, does
26   not change, and can be used to commit myriad financial crimes.
27

1            23. Because of the highly sensitive and personal nature of the information
2    Defendant acquires, stores, and has access to, Defendant, upon information and
3    belief, promised to, among other things: keep PII private; comply with industry
4    standards related to data security and PII; inform individuals of their legal duties
5    and comply with all federal and state laws protecting PII; only use and release PII
6    for reasons that relate to medical care and treatment; and provide adequate notice
7    to impacted individuals if their PII is disclosed without authorization.
8            24. By obtaining, collecting, using, and deriving a benefit from Plaintiff’s
9    and Class Members’ PII, Defendant assumed legal and equitable duties and knew
10   or should have known that it was responsible for protecting Plaintiff’s and Class
11   Members’ PII from unauthorized disclosure.
12           25. Plaintiff and the Class Members have taken reasonable steps to
13   maintain the confidentiality of their PII.
14           26. Plaintiff and the Class Members relied on Defendant to implement and
15   follow adequate data security policies and protocols, to keep their PII confidential
16   and securely maintained, to use such PII solely for business purposes, and to
17   prevent the unauthorized disclosures of the PII.
18   B.     Defendant Fails to Safeguard Consumer PII
19           27. On or around April 14, 2025, Defendant notified some customers, and
20   the Vermont Attorney General, that it ““identified suspicious online activity related
21   to your account.”2
22           28. Through Defendant’s investigation of the incident, it learned that “there
23   may have been suspicious log-in activity for a limited period of time… which may
24   have resulted in certain user account information being visible to the unauthorized
25   actor.” Thus, cybercriminals had unfettered access to Defendant’s systems for an
26

1    unknown period of time.
2          29. Defendant has not yet revealed the exact types of PII exposed in the
3    Data Breach, however, Defendant has confirmed that sensitive personal
4    information was included in the information compromised during the Data Breach.
5          30. It is likely the Data Breach was targeted at Defendant due to its status
6    as an entity that collects, creates, and maintains sensitive PII.
7          31. Upon information and belief, the cyberattack was expressly designed
8    to gain access to private and confidential data of specific individuals, including
9    (among other things) the PII of Plaintiff and the Class Members.
10         32. Upon information and belief, and based on the type of cyberattack, it is
11   plausible and likely that Plaintiff’s PII was stolen in the Data Breach. Plaintiff
12   further believes her PII was likely subsequently sold on the dark web following the
13   Data Breach, as that is the modus operandi of cybercriminals.
14         33. Defendant had a duty to adopt reasonable measures to protect
15   Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII from involuntary disclosure to third parties.
16         34. Because of the Data Breach, data thieves were able to gain access to
17   Defendant’s private systems, and were able to compromise, access, and acquire the
18   protected PII of Plaintiff and Class Members.
19         35. Defendant had obligations created by contract, industry standards,
20   common law, and its own promises and representations made to Plaintiff and Class
21   Members to keep their PII confidential and to protect them from unauthorized
22   access and disclosure.
23         36. Plaintiff and the Class Members reasonably relied (directly or
24   indirectly) on Defendant’s sophistication to keep their sensitive PII confidential; to
25   maintain proper system security; to use this information for business purposes only;
26   and to make only authorized disclosures of their PII.
27         37. Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ unencrypted, unredacted PII was
28                                           7
                                 CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
           Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF      Document 1      Filed 04/23/25    Page 8 of 38




1    compromised due to Defendant’s negligent and/or careless acts and omissions, and
2    due to the utter failure to protect Class Members’ PII. Criminal hackers obtained
3    their PII because of its value in exploiting and stealing the identities of Plaintiff and
4    Class Members. The risks to Plaintiff and Class Members will remain for their
5    respective lifetimes.
6    C.     The Data Breach was a Foreseeable Risk and Defendant were on Notice
7            38. Defendant’s data security obligations were particularly important given
8    the substantial increase in cyberattacks and/or data breaches in industries holding
9    significant amounts of PII preceding the date of the breach.
10           39. In light of recent high profile data breaches, Defendant knew or should
11   have known that their electronic records and PII they maintained would be targeted
12   by cybercriminals and ransomware attack groups.
13           40. Defendant knew or should have known that these attacks were common
14   and foreseeable.
15           41. In 2021, a record 1,862 data breaches occurred, resulting in
16   approximately 293,927,708 sensitive records being exposed, a 68% increase from
17   2020.3 The 330 reported breaches reported in 2021 exposed nearly 30 million
18   sensitive records (28,045,658), compared to only 306 breaches that exposed nearly
19   10 million sensitive records (9,700,238) in 2020.4
20           42. Therefore, the increase in such attacks, and attendant risk of future
21   attacks, was widely known to the public and to anyone in Defendant’s industry,
22   including Defendant.
23   D.     Defendant Fails to Comply with FTC Guidelines
24           43. The Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) has promulgated numerous
25   guides for businesses which highlight the importance of implementing reasonable
26

1    data security practices. According to the FTC, the need for data security should be
2    factored into all business decision-making.
3           44. In 2016, the FTC updated its publication, Protecting Personal
4    Information: A Guide for Business, which established cyber-security guidelines for
5    businesses. The guidelines note that businesses should protect the personal
6    customer information that they keep; properly dispose of personal information that
7    is no longer needed; encrypt information stored on computer networks; understand
8    its network’s vulnerabilities; and implement policies to correct any security
9    problems.5 The guidelines also recommend that businesses use an intrusion
10   detection system to expose a breach as soon as it occurs; monitor all incoming
11   traffic for activity indicating someone is attempting to hack the system; watch for
12   large amounts of data being transmitted from the system; and have a response plan
13   ready in the event of a breach.6
14          45. The FTC further recommends that companies not maintain PII longer
15   than is needed for authorization of a transaction; limit access to sensitive data;
16   require complex passwords to be used on networks; use industry-tested methods
17   for security; monitor for suspicious activity on the network; and verify that third-
18   party service providers have implemented reasonable security measures.
19          46. The FTC has brought enforcement actions against businesses for
20   failing to adequately and reasonably protect customer data, treating the failure to
21   employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect against unauthorized access
22   to confidential consumer data as an unfair act or practice prohibited by Section 5
23   of the Federal Trade Commission Act (“FTCA”), 15 U.S.C. § 45. Orders resulting
24   from these actions further clarify the measures businesses must take to meet their
25

1    data security obligations.
2          47. These FTC enforcement actions include actions against insurance
3    providers and partners like Defendant.
4          48. Defendant failed to properly implement basic data security practices.
5          49. Defendant’s failure to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to
6    protect against unauthorized access to customers and other impacted individuals’
7    PII constitutes an unfair act or practice prohibited by Section 5 of the FTC Act, 15
8    U.S.C. § 45.
9          50. Defendant was at all times fully aware of their obligation to protect the
10   PII. Defendant was also aware of the significant repercussions that would result
11   from their failure to do so.
12   E.   Defendant’s Breach
13         51. Defendant breached its obligations to Plaintiff and Class Members
14   and/or was otherwise negligent and reckless because it failed to properly maintain
15   and safeguard its computer systems and website’s application flow. Defendant’s
16   unlawful conduct includes, but is not limited to, the following acts and/or
17   omissions:
18                a.    failing to maintain an adequate data security system to reduce
19                      the risk of data breaches and cyber-attacks;
20                b.    failing to adequately protect PII;
21                c.    failing to properly monitor their own data security systems for
22                      existing intrusions;
23                d.    failing to ensure that their vendors with access to their computer
24                      systems and data employed reasonable security procedures;
25                e.    failing to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of electronic PII
26                      it created, received, maintained, and/or transmitted;
27                f.    failing to implement technical policies and procedures for
28                                             10
                                    CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
       Case 5:25-cv-03556-BLF       Document 1     Filed 04/23/25    Page 11 of 38




1                       electronic information systems that maintain electronic PII to
2                       allow access only to those persons or software programs that
3                       have been granted access rights;
4                g.     failing to implement policies and procedures to prevent, detect,
5                       contain, and correct security violations;
6                h.     failing to implement procedures to review records of information
7                       system activity regularly, such as audit logs, access reports, and
8                       security incident tracking reports;
9                i.     failing to protect against reasonably anticipated threats or
10                      hazards to the security or integrity of electronic PII;
11               j.     failing to train all members of their workforces effectively on the
12                      policies and procedures regarding PII;
13               k.     failing to render the electronic PII it maintained unusable,
14                      unreadable, or indecipherable to unauthorized individuals;
15               l.     failing to comply with FTC guidelines for cybersecurity, in
16                      violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act;
17               m.     failing to adhere to industry standards for cybersecurity as
18                      discussed above; and,
19               n.     otherwise breaching their duties and obligations to protect
20                      Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ PII.
21         52. Defendant negligently and unlawfully failed to safeguard Plaintiff’s
22   and Class Members’ PII by allowing cyberthieves to access Defendant’s online
23   insurance application flow, which provided unauthorized actors with unsecured and
24   unencrypted PII.
25         53. Accordingly, as outlined below, Plaintiff and Class Members now face
26   a present, increased risk of fraud and identity theft. In addition, Plaintiff and the
27   Class Members also lost the benefit of the bargain they made with Defendant.
28                                          11

1    F.     Data Breaches Cause Disruption and Increased Risk of Fraud and
2    Identity Theft
3            54. Cyberattacks and data breaches at financial companies like Defendant
4    are especially problematic because they can negatively impact the overall daily
5    lives of individuals affected by the attack.
6            55. The United States Government Accountability Office released a report
7    in 2007 regarding data breaches (“GAO Report”) in which it noted that victims of
8    identity theft will face “substantial costs and time to repair the damage to their good
9    name and credit record.”7
10           56. That is because any victim of a data breach is exposed to serious
11   ramifications regardless of the nature of the data. Indeed, the reason criminals steal
12   personally identifiable information is to monetize it. They do this by selling the
13   spoils of their cyberattacks on the black market to identity thieves who desire to
14   extort and harass victims, take over victims’ identities in order to engage in illegal
15   financial transactions under the victims’ names. Because a person’s identity is akin
16   to a puzzle, the more accurate pieces of data an identity thief obtains about a person,
17   the easier it is for the thief to take on the victim’s identity, or otherwise harass or
18   track the victim. For example, armed with just a name and date of birth, a data thief
19   can utilize a hacking technique referred to as “social engineering” to obtain even
20   more information about a victim’s identity, such as a person’s login credentials or
21   Social Security number. Social engineering is a form of hacking whereby a data
22   thief uses previously acquired information to manipulate individuals into disclosing
23   additional confidential or personal information through means such as spam phone
24   calls and text messages or phishing emails.
25           57. The FTC recommends that identity theft victims take several steps to

1    protect their personal and financial information after a data breach, including
2    contacting one of the credit bureaus to place a fraud alert (consider an extended
3    fraud alert that lasts for 7 years if someone steals their identity), reviewing their
4    credit reports, contacting companies to remove fraudulent charges from their
5    accounts, placing a credit freeze on their credit, and correcting their credit reports.8
6            58. Identity thieves use stolen personal information such as Social Security
7    numbers for a variety of crimes, including credit card fraud, phone or utilities fraud,
8    and bank/finance fraud.
9            59. Identity thieves can also use Social Security numbers to obtain a
10   driver’s license or official identification card in the victim’s name but with the
11   thief’s picture; use the victim’s name and Social Security number to obtain
12   government benefits; or file a fraudulent tax return using the victim’s information.
13   In addition, identity thieves may obtain a job using the victim’s Social Security
14   number, rent a house or receive medical services in the victim’s name, and may
15   even give the victim’s personal information to police during an arrest resulting in
16   an arrest warrant being issued in the victim’s name.
17           60. Moreover, theft of PII is also gravely serious because PII is an
18   extremely valuable property right.9
19           61. Its value is axiomatic, considering the value of “big data” in corporate
20   America and the fact that the consequences of cyber thefts include heavy prison
21   sentences. Even this obvious risk to reward analysis illustrates beyond doubt that
22   PII has considerable market value.

1             62. It must also be noted there may be a substantial time lag – measured in
2    years -- between when harm occurs and when it is discovered, and also between
3    when PII is stolen and when it is used.
4             63. According to the U.S. Government Accountability Office, which
5    conducted a study regarding data breaches:
6               [L]aw enforcement officials told us that in some cases, stolen data
                may be held for up to a year or more before being used to commit
7               identity theft. Further, once stolen data have been sold or posted
8               on the Web, fraudulent use of that information may continue for
                years. As a result, studies that attempt to measure the harm
9               resulting from data breaches cannot necessarily rule out all future
10              harm.10
11            64. PII is such a valuable commodity to identity-thieves that once the

12   information has been compromised, criminals often trade the information on the

13   “cyber black-market” for years.

14            65. There is a strong probability that entire batches of stolen information

15   have been dumped on the black market and are yet to be dumped on the black

16   market, meaning Plaintiff and Class Members are at an increased risk of fraud and

17   identity theft for many years into the future.

18            66. Thus, Plaintiff and Class Members must vigilantly monitor their

19   financial and medical accounts for many years to come.

20            67. PII can sell for as much as $363 per record according to the Infosec

21   Institute.11 PII is particularly valuable because criminals can use it to target victims

22   with frauds and scams. Once PII is stolen, fraudulent use of that information and

23   damage to victims may continue for many years.

24            68. For example, the Social Security Administration has warned that

25   identity thieves can use an individual’s Social Security number to apply for

1    additional credit lines.12 Such fraud may go undetected until debt collection calls
2    commence months, or even years, later. Stolen Social Security Numbers also make
3    it possible for thieves to file fraudulent tax returns, file for unemployment benefits,
4    or apply for a job using a false identity.13 Each of these fraudulent activities is
5    difficult to detect. An individual may not know that their Social Security Number
6    was used to file for unemployment benefits until law enforcement notifies the
7    individual’s employer of the suspected fraud. Fraudulent tax returns are typically
8    discovered only when an individual’s authentic tax return is rejected.
9             69. Moreover, it is not an easy task to change or cancel a stolen Social
10   Security number.
11            70. An individual cannot obtain a new Social Security number without
12   significant paperwork and evidence of actual misuse. Even then, a new Social
13   Security number may not be effective, as “[t]he credit bureaus and banks are able
14   to link the new number very quickly to the old number, so all of that old bad
15   information is quickly inherited into the new Social Security number.”14
16            71. This data, as one would expect, demands a much higher price on the
17   black market. Martin Walter, senior director at cybersecurity firm RedSeal,
18   explained, “[c]ompared to credit card information, personally identifiable
19   information and Social Security Numbers are worth more than 10x on the black
20   market.”15
